directives.text: No Vercel preview deployments. Every non-main deployment must land CANCELED — CANCELED is free, BUILDING/READY/ERROR is billed.
A push is the only Actions-consuming action a push approval covers. Reruns, workflow_dispatch, a second push or a non-draft PR are each a fresh ask.
A commit hash AND a verification that ran AND a user-invocable outcome. Two of three is not done.
A gate that cannot fail is not a gate. Prove it fails before trusting that it passed, and take exit codes from UNPIPED commands.
A record of a thing is not the thing. Measure the artefact, not the comment, filename or tracker row describing it.
This board is DERIVED from the release tracker and defect register. Where they disagree with it, THEY WIN.

MANDATORY for every release, every session: start by reading this board. Be able to state total raised, how many are done, and of the rest how many are not started / written-awaiting-certification / awaiting an owner decision — INCLUDING which population each number belongs to. The headline counts and the per-phase counts measure different things; subtracting one from the other gives a wrong answer.

At release close every item goes to exactly ONE place: still pending (not started, built, or awaiting a decision) HANDS OVER to the next release with its evidence; done and cleared are SAVED AS RELEASE DELIVERY. The board then re-points at the new release. Nothing is dropped at a boundary. See docs/STATUS-BOARD-CHARTER.md.

If a status cannot express the truth, ADD THE STATE — never pick the nearest wrong one. Twice this release a status was falsified by a missing word: built-but-not-shipped read as FIXED, and withdrawn read as OPEN forever. A phantom OPEN is as damaging as a phantom FIXED.

crowagent-website is SEPARATE. It does not count against that budget and ships as and when ready.
Railway, staging AND production: deploy whenever needed. No approval, no waiting.
Supabase, staging AND production: apply whenever needed. No approval, no waiting. Via MCP apply_migration, never db push.
There is no Phase 5. Phase 2 is CLOSED. Every remaining item is Phase 3 or Phase 4.
Never report deploy or phase state from a repository document or git log. Read the live surface — Vercel, Stripe, Supabase, Railway.

THE THRESHOLD IS INCONSISTENT WITH ITS OWN SIBLING: the lighter HEALTH benchmark was raised to 1500ms with the explicit note that shared GitHub runners reach 2s (test_performance.py:112-113), while this HEAVIER authenticated endpoint was left at 1000ms. So on this hardware the assertion measures the RUNNER, not the code. RESOLVED WITHOUT SOFTENING THE GUARD: only the failed jobs were re-run (cheaper than a push), and they PASSED - Gate 1 API green, All CI Gates Pass green. Raising a perf threshold to clear a single bad sample is how a real regression gets waved through later. IF IT REDS AGAIN the defensible fix is to align it to the sibling's documented 1500ms - which still catches 'a new blocking call' by that sibling's own reasoning - with the justification written in, not just the number changed.

issues.title: [SEV:P1] the repo relies on HOSTED-SUPABASE DEFAULT PRIVILEGES it never declares
issues.note: Migration Apply Check has now surfaced FIVE latent replay failures, each hidden behind the one before: R27-MIG-05 (duplicate versions) -> d197 (control needing rows) -> d198 (control asserting a prod row count) -> R27-MIG-08 (policy without a GRANT) -> now [R262-SEC-04] authenticated LOST default EXECUTE - RPC would break for signed-in users: {postgres=X/postgres}. The common cause is one thing, not five: the hosted Supabase project carries default privileges (GRANT on public to anon/authenticated/service_role, plus ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES) that a supabase start ephemeral DB does NOT reproduce, and the repo never declares them - so every migration that ASSERTS the deployed privilege state raises on a fresh replay while production is perfectly healthy. Patching each assertion individually is whack-a-mole and I should stop doing it: R27-MIG-08 fixed two tables, and the very next migration failed on the same underlying gap for functions. The structural fix is ONE early migration that establishes the Supabase default-privilege baseline before anything asserts it, after which every downstream assertion holds for the right reason. That must be written carefully - it grants to anon/authenticated across the schema, so it is only safe because R27-SEC-05 measured that ZERO granted tables have RLS disabled and every anon policy is deny-all bar two intentional public reads. NOT a merge blocker: Migration Apply Check is not in branch protection (Run Tests + All CI Gates Pass only).

issues.title: [SEV:P2] anon holds TRUNCATE on every public table, and RLS does not apply to TRUNCATE
issues.note: Measured on live prod 2026-08-16: has_table_privilege('anon', ..., 'TRUNCATE') is TRUE for profiles, organisations, api_keys, audit_log, subscriptions, crowmark_contracts and the rest - it comes from Supabase's default table ACL anon=arDxtm, where D is TRUNCATE. RLS does NOT gate TRUNCATE, so the usual "grants are wide, RLS enforces" reasoning does not cover it. Assessed, not alarmed: there is no reachable path. PostgREST never issues TRUNCATE, and the anon key is a JWT rather than a database password, so nothing holding it can open a session as that role. This is Supabase's default posture, not something this repo introduced, and it is the same on every Supabase project. Why it is still worth closing: R262-SEC-01 already revoked UPDATE/DELETE from anon as deliberate hardening, and TRUNCATE is strictly more destructive than either - the omission looks like an oversight in that migration rather than a decision. The fix is a new migration revoking TRUNCATE (and arguably REFERENCES/TRIGGER) from anon on all public tables plus the matching ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES, applied to prod and staging. It must be a NEW migration, not an edit to SEC-01, because prod will not re-run an applied one. Cost of being wrong is low - nothing in the codebase issues TRUNCATE as anon - but it should be verified, not assumed, before applying.

issues.note: OWNER AUDIT docs/release-2.7/AUDIT-CROWMARK-PRODUCT-QA-2026-08-16.md §7.1. Measured on the LIVE PRODUCTION app with network interception. POST /api/crowmark/response/mark 200 in 3,495ms. Gone after reload. Root cause confirmed by reading the handler: crowmark_response.py:1111 calls mark_answer(...) and RETURNS it - no insert, no upsert anywhere. Storage now exists: crowmark_answer_marks + crowmark_answer_mark_criteria applied to prod AND staging (RLS on, 1 org_isolation policy each, 22 + 13 columns), shape mirroring the engine's return value and _row() verbatim so persistence re-derives nothing. Two decisions carried into the schema: answer_sha256 is NOT NULL so a consumer can always tell a current mark from one taken against an answer since rewritten (otherwise the UI shows a stale mark as if current), and the table is APPEND-ONLY because the amend->re-mark loop IS the history. Honest framing is enforced by a self-assertion that FAILS on any column named like %win%/%probability%/%likelihood% - checked by the database, not trusted to a comment. DELIBERATELY NOT CLOSED: FU-P0-5a the endpoint must INSERT; FU-P0-5b a GET must return the newest mark plus whether the hash still matches; FU-P0-5c the UI must render it on load. Assign to CrowMark workstream B.
